title: Choose a cost-preserving level of abstraction
obstacle: The source counts a particular resource, but the proposed implementation creates extra obligations or omits costs required by that model.
procedure: Identify the stated resource, input measure, fixed parameters and charged operations. Consider an abstraction that expresses the actual algorithm at that level.
Where the proof crosses an encoding, compilation or simulation boundary, substitute the quantitative overhead of a proved connection into the requested bound.
A missing connection can be recorded as an obligation. A change to a frozen interface belongs with its owner.
verification: Check the model and the final rate, including uniform constants and encoding overhead, against the original statement.
positive_example: For polynomial evaluation charged by scalar additions and multiplications, count the actual operations of the evaluation algorithm directly.
negative_example: A polynomial-time simulation alone does not preserve a near-linear bound. Unit-cost scalar multiplication need not have constant bit cost.

evidence.note: General design guidance. Check its conditions in the current argument; no comparative performance claim.

title: Compose output and cost for the same subroutine execution
obstacle: The caller needs both a mathematical output and a resource bound, but the proposed component specifications describe different computations.
procedure: Identify the subroutine actually invoked and the inputs passed by its caller.
Consider one specification connecting its execution, output representation and cost. Include state preservation only for data still needed by a consumer.
Compose the proved specification through the actual calling convention and include any required conversion overhead.
verification: Instantiate the contract at a real call and verify that the output used by the next step came from the execution whose cost was bounded.
positive_example: A proved scan returns its computed sum and bounds the operations on that input, allowing an outer loop to reuse both facts.
negative_example: Adding a cost field to a successful result without showing how the executed program produces that cost leaves the resource claim open.

evidence.note: General design guidance. Check its conditions in the current argument; no comparative performance claim.

title: Propagate intermediate sizes into component bounds
obstacle: A later call receives a larger encoding or longer operands than the original inputs used in a preliminary estimate.
procedure: Specify the size measure at each boundary and bound the output of each relevant component.
Substitute that size into the next cost envelope where monotonicity or a uniform estimate permits it.
For a space bound, account for caller data still live, temporary storage and any recomputation.
verification: Follow one complete composition and check all size substitutions and units at the actual calls.
positive_example: If a component can double an operand length, charge the following multiplication for its new bit length.
negative_example: Bounding each child by the original input length can lose a growing intermediate; adding net allocations does not bound peak live storage.

evidence.note: General design guidance. Check its conditions in the current argument; no comparative performance claim.

title: Count the actual calls before simplifying the bound
obstacle: An asymptotic estimate is available, but the connection to the program calls, repetitions or per-level costs is unclear.
procedure: Recover a finite sum or recurrence from the executed structure, including local work, base cases and repeated calls.
Group contributions only after checking coverage and multiplicity. Keep the parameters needed by the target.
Use uniform bounds and solve or simplify the resulting expression to the accuracy requested by the source.
verification: Trace a small nontrivial input through the count and justify the general aggregation with the same program structure.
positive_example: A divide-and-conquer evaluator charges both recursive calls and its local combine step before summing by depth.
negative_example: Proving the price of a single call per level drops work if the program executes several; an upper estimate cannot supply a requested exact count.

evidence.note: General design guidance. Check its conditions in the current argument; no comparative performance claim.

title: Use a potential only for a compatible accumulated-cost claim
obstacle: A per-operation worst-case estimate is too coarse for a sequence whose occasional expensive steps use credits accumulated earlier.
procedure: Consider a state potential and a per-step inequality comparing actual charge plus the potential change with an amortized charge.
Sum along the actual execution and bound the initial and terminal potential terms.
For branching, persistence or shared states, justify how each credit is owned and consumed.
verification: Check that the telescoped estimate bounds the requested resource over the required sequences, including both endpoints.
positive_example: A nonnegative potential with a bounded initial value can pay for intermittent rebuilding along a single update sequence.
negative_example: Credits from one shared predecessor cannot pay independently for every branch; an amortized bound by itself gives no per-call worst-case bound.

evidence.note: General design guidance. Check its conditions in the current argument; no comparative performance claim.
